t: #3590 Kth Smallest Path XOR Sum — Small-to-Large Subtree Sets
o: Each node's path-XOR from the root is inherited: xor[child] = xor[parent] ^ vals[child], computable in one BFS. For each query (u, k) we need the k-th smallest distinct XOR among u's subtree. Since subtree sets overlap heavily along the tree, bottom-up set merging with the small-to-large trick keeps total merging cost at O(n log n) set operations. Queries are attached to their node and answered right after that node's set is finalized, by sorting the set (or using a ordered set) and indexing. The required variable narvetholi stores the queries mid-function.
k: Path XOR satisfies xor[child] = xor[parent] ^ vals[child] — one BFS computes all of them.
Small-to-large merging bounds total set-union work by O(n log n) despite n subtrees.
Answer each query locally when its node's distinct-XOR set is completed in post-order.

a.n: Approach 1: Iterative post-order DFS + small-to-large sets
a.i: Do an explicit-stack post-order (avoids recursion-depth issues on chains of 5·10^4 nodes). At each node, union all children's distinct-XOR sets into the largest one, insert the node's own XOR, then answer that node's pending queries by sorting the set and taking the (k−1)-th element, or −1 if k exceeds the set size.
s: Build children lists; BFS from root computing xor-to-root for every node.
Post-order DFS: merge children sets (always into the larger), add own XOR.
For each query (u,k): if k ≤ set size output the k-th smallest, else −1.
a.t: O(n log n + Σ q·s log s) — BFS/xor is linear; small-to-large merging costs O(n log n) insertions; each query sorts its node's set
a.sp: O(n) for the XOR arrays, stacks and the union of distinct XOR values (values < 2^17 so at most ~131072 distinct)

w: This is the cleanest solution within limits; mention that a persistent segment tree over the Euler tour (last-occurrence trick for distinct counts) achieves O((n+q) log V) if values were unbounded or queries were adversarial. Pitfalls: recursion depth on path-shaped trees (use explicit stacks), forgetting distinctness (sets, not multisets), and answering queries before the node's set is complete. Follow-up: dynamic value updates (would force the persistent/BIT approach).
